The artificial intelligence boom is putting unprecedented pressure on global energy grids. The energy needs of planned data centers outstrip planned energy additions in many places where hyperscalers are developing massive campuses. As a result, the private and public sector alike are increasingly and urgently adopting an all-of-the-above approach to energy development, increasing the scale and lifespan of fossil fuels and renewable energies alike, while also pouring funding into the research and development of next-gen energy alternatives.

One of those promising energy alternatives is enhanced geothermal. Geothermal energy itself is nothing new – about 85 percent of all houses in Iceland have been heated with geothermal energy for years now. But that kind of geothermal energy is only viable in geologically anomalous places like Iceland, where the heat from the Earth’s core naturally breaks through to the surface in the form of hot springs, geysers, or other forms of heat vents. But the emerging field of enhanced geothermal seeks to make geothermal energy viable anywhere on Earth by digging deep enough to access that heat and pump it to the surface.

In order to do that, geothermal startups and research projects are borrowing technology from a sector that knows a whole lot about drilling – Big Oil. That’s right, the next big thing in clean and green energy may come in the form of none other than fracking.

Hydraulic fracturing could allow geothermal initiatives to cost-effectively drill to extreme depths where thermal heat is naturally abundant in order to provide a source of zero-emissions energy 24 hours a day, seven days a week. “If you drill down deep enough — three, four, even six kilometers — you reach the point where the crust is uniformly hot,” University of California Irvine engineer Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi was quoted in a recent article from the UC Newsroom. “Then you can drill horizontally, create fractures, and pipe in water.” The rock heats the water, turning it to steam that can run turbines that generate electricity.

However, we still have a long way to go before that can be achieved at a commercially viable scale. “There is more than enough potential geothermal energy underground to power the entire United States, but unlocking it safely and economically is still a major challenge,” Qomi went on to say.

Scientists at the University of California are one of many groups trying to find a pathway toward bringing enhanced geothermal out of lab-based modeling and into the market. Some private companies are likewise working on employing hydraulic fracturing technology to unlock commercial enhanced geothermal. Meanwhile, others are employing techniques from the field of nuclear fusion, using a vacuum-tube gyrotron to vaporize rock molecules with high-frequency electromagnetic waves down a borehole.

The round-the-clock energy potential of enhanced geothermal is just one of the sector’s benefits. Another critical advantage of the sector is its broad, bipartisan appeal as one of the vanishingly few forms of clean energy to receive equally enthusiastic policy support under the Biden and Trump administrations. The UC project is backed by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission as part of this push.

The Department of Energy is bullish about the potential of geothermal in the future of the United States’ energy mix. Projections from the agency state that enhanced geothermal projects could provide about 90 gigawatts of carbon-free energy in the U.S. by 2050, or approximately enough to power at least 65 million homes.

Big Tech is also throwing its weight behind enhanced geothermal research and development. Quaise Energy, a startup employing the fusion-derived gyrotron approach, just signed a major power purchase agreement with Google to supply 50 megawatts (MW) of superhot geothermal power, beginning as soon as 2030. The deal stands as a major vote of confidence in the nascent sector.
